messages.subject_clean: Identical estimates in mark-resight by session
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am hopeful someone can point me in the right direction here. I am trying to fit a mark-resight model with multiple sessions to estimate deer density using camera traps. However when fitting the model to obtain a separate estimate for each session, I am ending up with identical estimates for all parameters for both sessions.

Question #1. Am I specifying the model for mark resight data correctly? The number of cameras and layout is different in each session, so I first read in both detector files (in order), and then specify those in the trapfile argument. My "deer_reduced.txt" file contains detections of known individuals at cameras in each session (sessionyear2021 and sessionyear2022). There are 30 occasions in each session, but no marking occasions as all individuals were marked prior to the sampling occasions. Its also worth noting that estimates seem extremely low, compared to when I fit each year individually. I've attached the data files, as well as the relevant code and results here:

CODE:
#read in camera trap files - order matters here!
camera_names = c(file.path(input_directory, "deer_cameras_2021.txt"),
                 file.path(input_directory, "deer_cameras_2022.txt"))

#Prepare the capthist object
deer_multisession<-read.capthist(captfile = file.path(input_directory, "deer_reduced.txt"),
              trapfile = camera_names,
              detector = "count",
              markocc = rep(0,30),
              skip = 1,
              verify = TRUE)
summary(deer_multisession, terse = TRUE)

start_time<-Sys.time()
#Fit the model
multisession_fit<-secr.fit(deer_multisession,
                           model = D ~ session, #lowercase "session" to fit a value for each level of session
                           details = list(autoini = 2), #Was having getting started unless I specify
                           buffer = 500,
                           trace = TRUE)
#I just like to know how long this takes
end_time<-Sys.time()
end_time - start_time

#Inspect results
summary(multisession_fit)

Question #2. I've tried playing with the simulation functions in secr, but again am running into difficulties with the sim.resight and sim.capthist. First, does sim.resight allow simulating multiple sessions? I am thinking no, so I have tried sim.capthis but am encountering a similar problem. When I simulate a capthist object with a single marking occasion and then fit "D~session"  I get reasonable estimates:

CODE:

markocc(grid)<-c(1,0,0,0,0)
#

                       nsessions = 2, renumber = FALSE,
            popn = list(D = 30), seed = 123)

               model = D~session,
               buffer = 500,trace = TRUE)

summary(fit0)

messages.subject_clean: extrapolating plots for whole colony.
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've written to the group previously about mark recapture on threatened snails on the island of Guam, and have a few more questions.

I have used SECR for the data and we mark the capture locations with GPS (Trimble) that is  supposed to get 10cm accuracy with a post processing of the data. However we do get inaccurate GPS points, shown by points for snails in areas next to the plot that we didn't search. The plots are small (10mx10m and 10mx15m). Some points show up just off of the plot boundaries and if we extend the boundaries of the plot then the data will run on SECR. Is it ok to do that, or does this bias the estimate? Some points are to far off of the plot so we just discard those.

We have delineated the colony and know that it covers 3ha. The delineation was done by walking transects next to each other and recording snail locations with GPS and then mapping those locations. We have 4 plots that we monitor. If we analyzed the mark recapture data in program MARK would it be possible to estimate the size of the colony by extrapolating the MARK numbers as a percentage of the total colony area. So if the 4 mark recapture plots cover 1450 square meters and and the MARK estimate is 500 snails can we extrapolate this number as 4.83 percent of the total (1450/30000)?

Understood the plots sample a bigger area than what the plot measurements are but, the area of the colony will also be bigger than the delineated area for the same reason and would not be estimating a density with the MARK numbers but as a percentage of the area that has been sampled.

Not sure if the above makes sense or not.

would love to hear opinions on this. I'm guessing I'm wrong but want to hear why.

Scott

messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott
The issue of GPS error is an interesting one that has been around a while without anyone investigating it to my knowledge (e.g., the coordinates used by Royle and Young 2008 must have had some error like this). I always assumed it would just inflate estimates of sigma, but boundary crossing is also a problem as you point out. It would be good to put some effort into describing the actual GPS error - then some simulations will lead to a concrete answer. I would be inclined to find a way of 'adjusting' or rejecting impossible locations, rather than expanding the nominal search area.

Regarding the merit of extrapolation from non-spatial (MARK) C-R estimates: it depends on the movements. The edge effect on your plots must be very different to (larger than) the edge effect on the enclosing area, so the logic is a bit weak, especially if movements are large.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
My advice was to document the distribution of GPS errors, so that could form the basis for a decision on what to do. My preference for editing points over expanding the nominal plot is not based on evidence, just a suspicion that expanding the plot is more damaging because it affects the data as a whole. You really should simulate a detection process in which long-tailed error is added to locations, and compare the effect of different rules. If it is too late to measure the actual error then simulate a range.

# code to simulate polygon-search data with error
# rx is anything - not used
onesim <- function (rx, D = 1e3, traps = testpoly,
                    detectpar = list(lambda0 = 0.5, sigma = 10),
                    noccasions = 5, error = 5,
                    plt = FALSE, fit = TRUE) {
    pop <- sim.popn(D, traps, model2D = 'poisson', buffer = detectpar$sigma*5)
    ch <- sim.capthist(traps, pop, detectfn = 'HHN', detectpar = detectpar, noccasions = noccasions)
    ###################
    # add error to locations
    n <- nrow(xy(ch))
    theta <- runif(n) * 2 * pi
    r <- rexp(n, 1/error)
    xyerror <- data.frame(x = r*cos(theta), y = r*sin(theta))
    xy(ch) <- xy(ch) + xyerror
    ###################
    if (plt) {
        plot(ch, varycol=F, border=50)
        print(c(n = n, outside = n-sum(pointsInPolygon(xy(ch), traps))))
    }
    if (fit) {
        predict(secr.fit(ch, detectfn = 'HHN', buffer = 40, verify = FALSE))
    }
    else {
        ch
    }
}
library(secr)
testpoly <- make.poly()
# show one example
onesim(1, plt = TRUE, fit = FALSE)
plot(testpoly, add=T, detpar = list(col=NA))

setNumThreads(4)
fits <- lapply(1:10, onesim)

# density estimates
mean(sapply(fits, '[', 1,2))
# [1] 956.4318

# sigma estimates
mean(sapply(fits, '[', 3,2))
# [1] 11.43191

Hi Marcela,

I'm quite late to this but just sharing some experiences with long surveys and multisession models in case useful.

It sounds like your post has two parts. One is how to get this analysis to run in secr. The other is about whether a multisession approach is a good idea for your data.

I couldn't see your attachments so feel free to repost or send them offline and I can try to help with the first. The multisession vignette (https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/SECRinR.html) is useful if you haven't seen that already. You likely do have count detectors and in that case the definition of occasion isn't important because data gets collapsed into a single occasion per session.

About the general suitability, I've used multisession models for data similar to yours where cameras have been left out for a long time and sample sizes are small, in a similar way to what you propose. I think it can be justified but you have to pretty careful because SECR models assume that populations are closed within session and independent between sessions, and when you split up a longer survey into sessions with no gaps between sessions you almost certainly violate at least one of those assumptions.

The trade-off is that you get a bigger sample size relative to what you'd get with a single session, or sessions separated by enough time that independence is reasonable. Sometimes that makes the crucial difference between getting a model to fit at all and not. In those cases the correct response is probably that the data aren't sufficient for SECR, but that can be pretty tough to hear after a big survey effort and I've not been brave enough to try it! So I guess I see the approach you outline as a pragmatic approach to an imperfect situation. Open population models are also an option, but tricky with small samples and more complicated in general.

If you do go this route there are a bunch of related choices, like how long your sessions should be, whether you can afford to have gaps between sessions, your choice of time 'origin', and whether parameters should be session-specific or shared. The multisession vignette says confidence intervals will be too narrow, so there's also that to consider. Basically the approach isn't without issues but awareness of those issues, being able to motivate your choices of e.g session length, and running plenty of checks to see how sensitive your results are to these choices will go a long way. More generally I think it's a topic where a broader simulation study would be useful because the situation seems to come up reasonably often and there is limited guidance (perhaps because it's a bad idea).

Unrelated to the multisession stuff, six cameras (if I've read that correctly) is very few and that ultimately might make the data unsuitable for SECR. A rough guide is that you'd want enough cameras to at the very least cover an animal's typical home range with 1-2 sigma spacing between cameras. That can't be done with 6 cameras and so your ability to estimate sigma especially might be poor.

Hope that helps, good luck.

Ian

Greg
I think I've found where the wheels come off, pending your scenario data.frame.

If you specify group-specific sigma AND leave run.scenarios to construct the maskset THEN maskindex varies between groups within a scenario, which is not allowed. This can be fixed by specifying the masks (they can still differ between scenarios). I've added a more detailed error message to the code on GitHub that you can install with devtools::install_github("MurrayEfford/secrdesign") (if brave).

Murray

For example:
library(secrdesign)
scen <- make.scenarios(D = 5, trapsindex = 1:3, sigma = 25, g0 = 0.2, groups = 1:2)
scen$sigma <- c(20,30)[scen$group]  # group-specific sigma
traplist <- rep(list(make.grid()), 3)

# fails
sims <- run.scenarios(nrepl = 10, scenarios = scen, trapset = traplist,
                      ncores = 1, extractfn = identity)
# runs
scen$maskindex <- rep(1,nrow(scen))
masklist <- list(make.mask(traplist[[1]], buffer=100))
sims <- run.scenarios(nrepl = 10, scenarios = scen, trapset = traplist,
                      maskset = masklist, ncores = 1, extractfn = identity)

Hello all,

I am working on a study in Switzerland, where we employ camera traps to calculate the density of lynx per 100km2. So far, I have identified the site-specific learned response model Mbk as the best model using predefined models (while keeping the parameter sigma constant). As in mountainous landscape lynx movements are strongly influenced by the topography of the terrain, we are investigating the non-euclidean distances in secr;

I first used static userdist to add barriers to my mask (lakes), and now I'm attempting to perform a dynamic userdist. Specifically, I aim to model densities by accounting for non-Euclidean ecological distances determined by e.g. the Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI).

To account for the TRI, I believe I should use the code provided in the example 5 ‘Habitat model for connectivity’ of the dynamic userdist section in “Non-Euclidean distances in secr 4.6”, Murray Efford, 2023:

fit5 <- secr.fit(lynx_capthist, mask = Mask_NonEucDist_Lakes_1000b,

trace = FALSE,

details = list(userdist = fn2, fastproximity = FALSE),

model = list(D ~ 1, g0~bk, noneuc ~ TRI),

fixed = list(sigma = 1))

However, I am uncertain about the appropriate function to employ in userdist. Here the function fn2 (p.6 and written below) was used in the model to acknowledge that the “scale of movement σ depends on locations of both home-range centre and detector”. But I am not sure to understand the link between the function fn2 and the noneuc ~ TRI, what function should I use in the userdist when my aim is to account for how the terrain ruggedness could affect the lynx movements and detection probability…?

Also before trying fit5 above, I tried the fit2 (below) to test the fn2 function alone, but the loglik returns only NA, even when I change the starting value of the sigma parameter. However, I noticed that when I remove the “fixed = list(sigma = 1)the loglik returns values, and I “just” get the warning message “In secr.fit(lynx_capthist, mask = Mask_NonEucDist_Lakes_1000b, details = list(userdist = fn2,  : at least one variance calculation failed”.

  if (missing(xy1)) return("noneuc")

  xy1 <- addCovariates(xy1, mask)

  xy2 <- addCovariates(xy2, mask)

  sig1 <- as.numeric(covariates(xy1)$noneuc)

  sig2 <- as.numeric(covariates(xy2)$noneuc)

  euc <- edist(xy1, xy2)

trace = FALSE,

Thanks in advance for your help!

'fn2' averages the predicted sigma values at the start and end of a potential path; this is probably not what you want.

sigma is notionally fixed at a known value in the model (1), and the machinery of non-euclidean distance in effect  models variation in sigma relative to that fixed value. This is partly explained in the Notes of the pdf.

messages.body_plain:
Oliver

Thanks for sending example data that allowed me to find the source of the 'negative length vector' error. Turns out that the product of the dimensions of an internal array exceeded the allowed size of integer in R. I have added an explicit error message, now on GitHub. In your case it reads
Error: integer overflow in open.secr.loglifkn: 4667 parameter levels is too many given the numbers of detectors (1811) and mask cells (1949)
The code prepares a large array with size equal to the product of these dimensions, in your case 16472825213 (the largest integer allowed is about 2*10^9 - see ?as.integer). So you would need to reduce the number of parameter combinations by a factor of about 10 for it to work. I have yet to look into how you might do this.

The 'number of parameter levels' is the number of unique combinations of the levels of the different predictor variables. (Perhaps 'parameter' is misused here - may change that). I imagine the problem is the escalating number of unique combinations when predictors are combined, rather than the number of predictor variables per se.

Thinking aloud: Modelling spatial variation in phi is a hard problem because, conceptually, you would need to integrate over the possible unknown locations of animals between capture times and after last capture. Perhaps go down the Nimble path? Or partition your data according to first-capture location (I've just done this in another study)? (Most of your animals are in one clump, so chasing spatial effects may be unsatisfying). The CJSsecr model is messy because despite the name it's not a direct analogue of non-spatial CJS. I see why you would want to use it, but I don't think we (I) understand its limits.

I suggest using 'HEX' instead of 'HHR'. Failure with halfnormal (HHN) probably reflects the extreme improbability of distant detections under that model; HEX allows occasional long movements without requiring an extra parameter (HHR also leads to buffer-dependence, but that is probably not an issue for you).

Murray
